items.title: Elon Musk spends about an hour a week on his $16 billion foundation. Most of its 2025 giving went to another Musk nonprofit
items.summary:
Elon Musk’s foundation gave away nearly $400 million in 2025, and more than three-quarters of it went to another nonprofit he founded, according to the Musk Foundation’s latest tax filing , first reported by Bloomberg.

That total is down from the record $474 million the foundation gave in 2024. Over the same year, its assets grew by more than $1 billion, to about $16 billion, helped by a $64 million gift of Tesla shares. That makes it one of the world’s largest private foundations.

The gap between what the foundation holds and what it gives matters because private foundations must generally pay out about 5% of their investment assets each year or face IRS excise taxes . The Musk Foundation has fallen short of that minimum before, Forbes reported after reviewing its 2024 filing . Foundations can make up a shortfall the following year, so one year’s giving doesn’t settle whether the rule was met.

The foundation runs with almost no staff. Its tax return lists three directors: Musk, his family-office head Jared Birchall, and Matilda Simon. Musk, who is also listed as president, reported working for the foundation about an hour a week, Bloomberg reported.

Where the money went 

More than $310 million went to The Foundation, a nonprofit Musk set up to run a STEM-focused primary and secondary school in Bastrop, Texas, outside Austin, with plans to eventually add a university .

Another $20 million went to a donor-advised fund at Fidelity Charitable over which Musk has advisory control. Donors to these funds can take a tax deduction when they contribute and later recommend…
items.t: Elon Musk spends about an hour a week on his $16 billion foundation. Most of its 2025 giving went to another Musk nonprofit

items.title: The stock market faces a worrying scenario: a sell-off with no flight to safety
items.summary:
In today’s CEO Daily: Why AI stocks could be volatile for some time 

The big leadership story: Is the fabled singularity finally here? 

The markets: S&P 500 futures are up, even as Asia continues to sink 

Plus: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune . 

Good morning . U.S. markets are in correction territory, with the S&P 500 down more than 11% since its October highs, and the Nasdaq Composite down about 18%. Take your pick of culprits: AI spending, the Nvidia turmoil, trade tensions, the midterm fallout, sticky inflation. 

While S&P 500 futures suggest there could be a bounce today, stocks could be volatile for some time. Here’s what to watch:

The AI ecosystem. Nvidia shares kept sliding, but the pain also spread to stocks like Caterpillar , which now trades like an AI infrastructure stock because so much of its growth comes from data centers. The company’s stock fell 5% Friday and is down about 28% over the past month. Data center opposition was a winning issue in several midterm races, meaning future deals could face more friction. For those who supply cooling equipment, power generation and other data center infrastructure, the question is which companies already have financing and approval. Nvidia’s deals with specialized AI cloud providers, or neoclouds, are contingent on those customers securing financing. And Nvidia itself is backing deals, though the details are often fuzzy, making it hard to predict how Nvidia’s lower valuation ripples through customers whose deals depend on its backing.

The bond market. When investors flee stocks, they often shift…
items.t: The stock market faces a worrying scenario: a sell-off with no flight to safety

items.title: Morgan Freeman says AI should do ‘what we actually are dreaming of doing’—but deepfakes have also made him say things he never said
items.summary:
Morgan Freeman has arguably the most recognizable voice in Hollywood—and that’s made him a frequent target for AI copycats.

“You can create artists and make them say things they never said, which has happened to me,” Freeman told Fortune . 

Freeman isn’t against the technology itself. He and longtime producing partner Lori McCreary have spent decades putting new tools to work in filmmaking through their movie production company, Revelations Entertainment. The issue, he said, is privacy.

“What we should be doing with technology is what we actually are dreaming of doing,” he said. “But we have to somehow protect privacy, and that’s the first thing that loses its grip.”

McCreary, who cofounded Revelations Entertainment with Freeman in 1996, said AI is different from the tools that came before it. About two and a half years ago, she came across a clip online she didn’t remember Freeman filming, so she called to ask him about it. 

“He was like, ‘I don’t remember.’ And that was the first time when I thought, ‘Okay, we’ve got to get ahead of this,’” McCreary told Fortune .

Freeman has pushed back about AI copies of his voice, too. Last November, Freeman told The Guardian his lawyers had been “very, very busy” and had found “quite a few” instances of his voice being replicated without his consent. And in June 2024, he also thanked fans on X for calling out unauthorized AI imitations of his voice. 

McCreary said they now get calls every day about people selling products online using Freeman’s voice, which he has no connection to. AI can reproduce his voice and his…
items.t: Morgan Freeman says AI should do ‘what we actually are dreaming of doing’—but deepfakes have also made him say things he never said

items.title: After the Palisades fire, a founder built AI to help survivors with paperwork. Now he needs a state to buy it
items.summary:
When the Palisades fire tore through his Los Angeles neighborhood in January 2025, Jonathon Nostrant’s house was damaged but still standing. Many of his neighbors’ homes were destroyed.

The fire was only the first ordeal. Next, Nostrant found a tangle of federal, state, and local assistance programs, each with its own forms, eligibility rules, and deadlines. Survivors with insurance must also report their payouts to every agency they apply to, because FEMA cannot pay for losses an insurer already covers.

Insurance was already a sore subject in the Palisades. A year before the fire, State Farm dropped roughly 1,600 policies in the neighborhood, Fortune reported as the fire burned .

“Our insurance was fighting with us,” Nostrant said in an interview, describing his own claim.

That experience led to AidFinder, a Miami-based startup Nostrant co-founded that uses AI to match disaster survivors with programs they may qualify for, explain eligibility rules, and prepare applications. Survivors review everything before submission. The intended customers, though, are states, which would offer the platform to residents under their own banner.

For now, it is a pitch. AidFinder hasn’t signed its first state customer, and survivors have yet to use the platform, Refresh Miami reported on Nov. 17 . Nostrant told the outlet the company is in talks with 30 states, including Florida, and that Craig Fugate, who ran FEMA under President Barack Obama, has accepted a seat on its board.

A voice-tech veteran takes on paperwork 

Nostrant has spent much of his career teaching machines to…
items.t: After the Palisades fire, a founder built AI to help survivors with paperwork. Now he needs a state to buy it

items.title: LinkedIn CEO warns the job market is ‘frozen’— but he says Gen Z could have the upper hand because employers may assume they’re AI-savvy
items.summary:
The entry-level job market is the worst it’s been in 37 years. Nearly 60% of fresh-faced grads are frozen out of the workforce. And leaders have warned an AI “ tsunami ” is coming which could leave Gen Z graduates stuck working at Starbucks . But LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero doesn’t buy that the generation is doomed to making latte art.

“It is a frozen job market, and that does make it tougher for people that are earlier in their career for sure,” Shapero exclusively told Fortune , before quickly adding the caveat that there “are advantages to being early in your career, in standing out in a job interview, particularly as companies try to embrace AI.” 

Ironically, AI is the very thing wiping out entry-level jobs, and it could also be what gets young people hired. Even if Gen Zers don’t actually know more about AI than their older colleagues, employers may assume they do—giving young job seekers an upper hand. 

“There is a belief that people that are earlier, maybe they’re more attuned to the latest tech, and they understand how to use AI in their job,” Shapero explains. “And a lot of companies are trying to hire people like that because they want to transform how the company operates. So I think there are advantages.”

He’s not wrong. Employers have consistently told Fortune that they’re looking for young talent, specifically because they’re digitally native.

‘I’m hiring entry-level because they have no boundaries or limitations’ 

Alon Chen, founder and CEO of Tastewise—a generative AI platform trusted by PepsiCo , Nestlé, and Mars—is also actively looking for Gen Zers…
items.t: LinkedIn CEO warns the job market is ‘frozen’— but he says Gen Z could have the upper hand because employers may assume they’re AI-savvy

items.title: The smartphone market is facing ‘the great disruption.’ Chinese giant Oppo senses an opportunity
items.summary:
The world’s first smartphone—the IBM Simon Personal Communicator—cost $899, took 90 minutes to charge and allowed you to make calls, send faxes, and read emails for an hour before you had to charge it again. In 1994 it was the business leaders’ success signal of choice. 

The IBM Simon sold 50,000 units and marked the start of a new market category that, via the Blackberry, Apple iPhone, and Android, has become an essential part of modern daily life. Roughly 90 per cent of people in the U.S., the U.K., and the European Union own or use a smartphone. 

Ultra-mature markets bring problems. Users tend to hang onto their phones for longer as the marginal improvement of each new model diminishes. In the battle for vital processing chips, smartphone players are reluctant to pay the high prices of AI-frontier labs and data centers. This has led to shortages in supply. 

“2026 is expected to mark the smartphone market’s largest contraction ever, with shipments forecast to decline 11.9%,” according to a report by Omdia, a technology researcher. “A further 6% decline is anticipated in 2027, which will mark the lowest annual volume since 2013—a period when the market still was in its expansion phase.” 

Step forward Oppo, a Chinese smartphone company which is fifth in the global market behind Apple, Samsung , Xiaomi , and Vivo. With America largely cut off from Chinese players it has opted to focus on expansion in Europe, with premium devices aimed at young people. The reasons why are illuminating. 

In the West, Chinese suppliers face a perception problem, particularly among older…
items.t: The smartphone market is facing ‘the great disruption.’ Chinese giant Oppo senses an opportunity

items.title: How Luana Lopes Lara built Kalshi into a $40 billion prediction market giant that overtook Polymarket
items.summary:
It’s Election Night 2026. Luana Lopes Lara has been preparing for this evening for at least three years. Fresh off a plane from the buttoned-up Futures Industry Association’s expo in Chicago, the 30-year-old on-paper billionaire heads straight to the downtown Manhattan offices of Kalshi, the $40 billion prediction market startup she cofounded that promises to change how we interact with the financial system and understand our future.

“Are the odds going to be everywhere? Are we going to have the best product?” Lopes Lara asks.

Her staff are waiting in a war room ready to order pizza, screens lighting up with constantly changing blue-and-red odds, a second-by-second accounting of all the trades on the Kalshi app. Will Democrats take the Senate? Kalshi’s market on that yes-or-no question is judging the odds at 76% yes, with more than $338 million collectively bet on the outcome. The Texas governor’s race market flips for underdog Democrat Gina Hinojosa, and someone screams—Lopes Lara and her team all huddle around to see what’s happened.

Kalshi and its competitor Polymarket provide an experience somewhere between betting on DraftKings and browsing X. Users put money down on any number of questions—Will the Buffalo Bills beat the Minnesota Vikings? Will Taylor Swift be seen with ex-friend Blake Lively by the end of the year? Will the price of Bitcoin increase in the next 15 minutes?— and receive a payout (or lose their money) when the answer is revealed, if they don’t cash out sooner. The technical term for these bets is an “event contract,” a form of trading regulated by…
items.t: How Luana Lopes Lara built Kalshi into a $40 billion prediction market giant that overtook Polymarket

items.title: Dodging space junk costs $58 million a year. Meet the Space Force contractor who made ‘autopilot for satellites’ to save money for taxpayers
items.summary:
Every time a satellite swerves around a piece of space junk, it can burn about $1 million worth of fuel, according to NASA . Across U.S. satellites, NASA says the cost of debris is about $58 million a year, most of it borne by military and civil spacecraft that taxpayers pay for.

That is what BQP—a Syracuse, N.Y., simulation company that began in India in 2020 and now works for the Space Force—is trying to solve. Earth orbit is filling up faster than Washington can decide who should police it. BQP says its software, which founder and CEO Abhishek Chopra calls “autopilot for satellites,” can cut that bill by letting spacecraft decide on their own when to move.

“It’s completed the ground testing successfully,” Chopra said of a test on a partner company’s hardware. “It’s actually flying to International Space Station to be tested in the real space environment.”

Abhishek Chopra, CEO of BQP. Courtesy of BQP 

A crowded orbit 

There’s a long history of spacecraft turning into trash—and authorities trying to enforce some accountability.

When NASA’s Skylab space station crashed over Western Australia in 1979, the Shire of Esperance fined the agency $400 for littering, but NASA never paid. And bills have only gotten bigger. In 1978, a Soviet satellite, Cosmos 954, scattered radioactive debris across Canada’s Northwest Territories. Canada billed Moscow about 6 million Canadian dollars and settled for 3 million. But the FCC didn’t fine a company over space debris until 2023, when it charged Dish Network $150,000 for parking a dead satellite in the wrong orbit.

Air travel faced…
items.t: Dodging space junk costs $58 million a year. Meet the Space Force contractor who made ‘autopilot for satellites’ to save money for taxpayers

items.title: Tokyo won’t fall as hard as Seoul or Taipei when the AI trade cools, says Japan Exchange Group CEO Hiromi Yamaji
items.summary:
Global AI stocks sold off sharply over the past week, following Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO and tighter rules around semiconductor exports. Not even Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO on Thursday revived sentiment. Tech-heavy indices fell sharply: the Nasdaq 100 fell 9.1% last week, while the PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index is down by 13% over the same period. 

Yet Hiromi Yamaji, CEO of the Japan Exchange Group (JPX), isn’t too worried about the tech turmoil hitting Japan too hard. 

“The weight of AI or semiconductor-related stocks in the TOPIX is only 11.3%… in the S&P 500 it’s 20%, in the Nasdaq100 it’s 27%, in Taiwan it’s 47%, and in Korea it’s 60%,” Yamaji tells Fortune . “If there is much less trading volume of AI-related stocks, then we will see some decrease in trading value, but the impact won’t be as much as in other markets.”

The TOPIX index, which covers the broader Japanese equity market and was developed by JPX, fell 7% last week. Japan’s other benchmark index, the Nikkei 225, dropped by 8% over the same period. (The Nikkei 225, developed by Nikkei Inc., tracks a smaller number of large Japanese companies, including more tech manufacturing companies).

Taiwan’s TAIEX index—where chipmaker TSMC makes up over 40% of the weight—crashed by 13% last week, prompting the island’s government to take measures against short-selling on Thursday to stabilize markets.

Japanese equities hit historic highs in the summer of 2026 following a series of corporate governance reforms Yamaji launched, which were aimed at improving market transparency and fairness. The…

Futures tied to the Dow Jones industrial average surged 798 points, or 1.66%. S&P 500 futures shot up 2.11%, and Nasdaq futures soared 2.75%.

That came after the Dow and Nasdaq notched their biggest weekly declines since the early days of the COVID-10 pandemic, while the S&P 500 saw its steepest such drop since April 2025, when President Donald Trump stunned markets with his “Liberation Day” tariffs.

The S&P 500 and Dow joined the Nasdaq in correction territory. Tech shares have led the selloff as Wall Street fears the AI boom is about to go bust. The downtrend began after the midterm elections handed victories to Democrats more skeptical of data centers.

But the Nvidia spy scandal that led to Jensen Huang’s ouster as CEO poured more fuel on the fire, igniting additional worries that his “circular” financing deals would unravel and leave neocloud companies in its ecosystem without capital for new data centers or AI chips.

In addition, revelations that China had backdoor access to high-end U.S. chips used in AI development are spurring a federal crackdown to close loopholes in export restrictions. Trump even vowed to stop U.S. companies from building data centers abroad.

Moody’s Analytics Chief Economist Mark Zandi warned in a social media post that the stock market selloff could weigh on economic growth via the wealth effect, which affects consumer spending.

items.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
items.summary:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of…
items.t: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris

Climate talks reached a standstill on Saturday night in Turkey as some countries mulled whether to force a showdown with Saudi Arabia and its allies over the global need to phase out fossil fuels.

The co-conveners of the Cop31 UN climate summit, Australia’s Chris Bowen and Turkey’s Murat Kurum, held meetings with scores of countries throughout Saturday until late evening as the fortnight-long talks overran without resolution, with countries and campaigners growing increasingly frustrated at the lack of progress.

items.title: I hated life as a Neet. But now I’ve found a job, life is just as precarious | Emilija Morrison
items.summary:
The government’s plans to help young people not in education, work or training are welcome – I dearly hope they offer long-term security

  • Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism

What child dreams of being unemployed when they grow up? You can probably remember the days, aged 10, when you were asked to present to the class what you wanted to be. Imagine hearing this: “I want to be unemployed. After I graduate from university, I want to go to the jobcentre in my home town and collect my benefits every month.”

Yet that is the reality for many young people today – childhood dreams to become a teacher, a doctor, an engineer or whatever other profession thwarted not by the limits of their abilities, but the reality of the economy.

Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.summary:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage
items.t: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
